notes.title: Start here: three decision records and the scheduler walkthrough
notes.body:
Stack Ready is a quiz app that teaches through questions, and its `upskilling/` folder teaches the senior judgement around it. Every document is tied to real lines of this codebase. "Before" always means the baseline commit `6f1bf43`; the working tree has moved on since, so a document may describe a bug that the current code has already fixed.

This pack draws on four documents. Read them in this order:

1. `upskilling/02-adrs/0002-grade-on-the-server-never-ship-the-key.md`: where grading happens, and what that costs.
2. `upskilling/02-adrs/0009-trimmed-sm2-mastery-is-two-reps.md`: the scheduling algorithm and the definition of mastery.
3. `upskilling/03-walkthroughs/02-srs-scheduler.md`: the scheduler line by line, with eleven behaviours to stop at.
4. `upskilling/02-adrs/0015-an-early-correct-answer-is-practice.md`: the fix for a gap the first two documents admit.

Each ADR has the same sections: Context, Decision, Evidence, Consequences, Alternatives rejected, Breaks first at, Revisit when. Most questions come from Consequences and Alternatives rejected. Keep `server/src/srs.js` open; it is short.

excerpts.quote: Every guide, decision record and journal entry is about a real line in `server/`, `client/` or `content/`, quoted at a named commit.
Every "before" in this folder refers to commit **`6f1bf43`** (main, 2026-09-23), the last commit before the refactor.

notes.title: Concept: a trimmed SM-2 in plain words
notes.body:
Spaced repetition shows you a card again just before you would forget it. Each correct answer pushes the next review further away; a wrong answer brings the card back soon.

This app keeps the shape of the classic SM-2 algorithm and cuts the rest:

- Each card has an **ease** factor that moves up a little after a correct answer and down after a wrong one, kept between a floor and a ceiling.
- The first intervals are fixed (1 day, then 3 days); after that each interval is the previous one multiplied by the ease.
- A wrong answer resets the card's **reps** and brings it back in 10 minutes.
- A card counts as **mastered** after two reps.

The walkthrough's contract section lists the invariants the function must keep: the input is never mutated, ease stays in range, and so on. Before reading the code, read that list, then try to point at the line that enforces each invariant.

excerpts.quote: We keep SM-2's shape (ease factor, growing intervals, reset on failure) and cut the rest.
Given a card's state, whether the answer was right, and the time, return the card's next state: when it is due again, how fast its intervals grow, and whether it now counts as mastered.

readMore.why: The contract and its five invariants.
Eleven behaviours, each with a line to point at.

notes.title: Concept: why the server grades, and what that buys
notes.body:
In this app the schedule, the XP and the stage unlocks are all computed from graded attempts. So the question "where does grading happen?" decides whether any of those numbers mean anything.

ADR-0002 answers it: the server removes the answer key and the explanation from each question before sending it, grades the submitted answer itself, and only then returns the teaching text. The browser never holds the key, so it cannot be read in DevTools or leaked by a stray log line.

Reading the ADR, notice the honest parts. Its Consequences section lists real costs, including one way the key still leaked despite never being sent. Its "Alternatives rejected" section explains why two tempting shortcuts were refused. An ADR that lists only benefits is a sales pitch; this one is a record of a trade-off.

excerpts.quote: The schedule, the XP and the stage unlocks are all computed from graded attempts, so where grading happens decides whether any of those numbers can be trusted.
We strip `answer`, `why` and `ask` from every question before it leaves the server, grade on the server, and return the teaching payload only in the response to an attempt.

readMore.why: The whole grading decision, including its costs.

notes.title: Why a correct answer is simply 'good'
notes.body:
Full SM-2 asks the learner to rate each answer from 0 to 5. That makes sense when you recall a fact from memory and can say how hard it felt. A multiple-choice quiz only knows **right or wrong**. Asking the learner to self-rate would add a decision to every single card, and the rating would not be honest information anyway. So the ADR maps every correct answer to quality "good" and rejects full SM-2 for exactly that reason.

Why the others are wrong:
- **quality applies only to cloze cards**: the ADR does not say this; its reason is the right/wrong signal.
- **a schema migration the table could not take**: storage is not mentioned as the reason.
- **learners would inflate XP with 5s**: the ADR's concern is speed and an honest signal, not XP cheating.

excerpts.quote: Real SM-2 asks for a 0–5 quality grade after each answer. A quiz has only right or wrong, and asking learners to self-rate would slow every card.
**Full SM-2 with self-rating.** It is one extra decision per card, for a signal a multiple-choice answer cannot give honestly.

notes.title: Why a hashed key in the browser is no secret
notes.body:
Hashing hides a value only when there are too many possibilities to guess. A multiple-choice question has maybe four choices. Anyone holding the hash can hash each of the four choices and see which one matches, so the "hidden" key is found almost instantly. That is why ADR-0002 rejects grading in the browser with a hashed key: the answer space is far too small for hashing to protect anything.

Why the others are wrong:
- **hashing is slow on phones**: hashing four short strings is instant; speed is not the issue.
- **the hash would change with the explanation**: the ADR's objection is brute force, not stored attempts.
- **browsers have no hash function**: browsers do have built-in hashing (Web Crypto); the ADR does not argue this.

excerpts.quote: **Grade in the browser with a hashed key.** The hash of a four-way choice is brute-forced by trying four values.

notes.title: Why not a minimum gap between answers
notes.body:
A minimum-gap rule ("ignore a correct answer if the last one was less than X ago") sounds simpler, but ADR-0015 rejects it for two reasons. First, any X is **arbitrary**: why 5 minutes and not 50? Second, it would clash with an existing rule: after a wrong answer the card comes back in 10 minutes for a relearn. A minimum gap could block that relearn. The chosen rule instead keys on the card's own `dueAt`, which the schedule already provides.

Why the others are wrong:
- **a replayed POST doubles XP**: the ADR lists blocking replays as a benefit of the practice rule, not as the reason a gap fails.
- **the clock is not injectable**: `schedule()` takes `now` as a parameter, so time is testable.
- **needs a new column and no migrations exist**: not the reason given.

excerpts.quote: **A minimum gap since the last answer.** It is arbitrary, and it blocks the 10-minute relearn after a lapse.
A wrong answer is a lapse (`reps > 0`) or a failure (`reps === 0`) at any time, due again in 10 minutes.

notes.title: At the baseline, two quick answers mastered a card
notes.body:
At `6f1bf43`, `schedule()` never looked at `state.dueAt`. Every correct answer added a rep, whenever it came. So two correct answers 60 seconds apart gave `reps 2`, and mastery is `reps >= 2`: the card was **mastered**. Sessions re-serve non-due cards on purpose (drills, "Another round"), so this was the normal path, not an edge case. Worse, the self-test checked it as a pass, calling `schedule` twice with the same `now`.

Why the others are wrong:
- **counted as a lapse**: a lapse needs a wrong answer; both answers were correct.
- **rejected with a 409**: nothing at the baseline rejected early answers.
- **reps kept at 1**: that is the fixed behaviour from ADR-0015 ("practice"), not the baseline.

excerpts.quote: **spacing is not enforced**: nothing in `schedule` reads `state.dueAt`. A correct answer 60 seconds after the first one advances `reps` to 2 and masters the card
state = schedule(state, true, now); check('second correct answer reaches mastery', isMastered(state));

notes.title: Why dueAt is the start of a local day
notes.body:
Suppose `dueAt` were exactly now plus 24 hours. You answer at 10:00 today; tomorrow you study a little earlier, at 09:55. The card shows as due "tomorrow", but under the practice rule an answer **before** `dueAt` is practice, so your correct answer moves nothing. Anyone who studies a bit earlier each day would get practice on every card. So for intervals of a day or more, `dueAt` is local midnight at the start of that day: "back in 1 day" means any time tomorrow. A test pins the 09:55 case as a rep.

Why the others are wrong:
- **served twice at 00:00**: not the problem the ADR describes.
- **180 days overflow the ISO string**: ISO dates hold far larger dates; 180 is a deliberate cap.
- **the relearn could not come back**: wrong answers use `now + 10 minutes` regardless of how day intervals are stored.

excerpts.quote: **Due to the millisecond.** It turns "back in 1 day" into practice for anyone who studies earlier than yesterday.

"Back in 1 day" means * answerable any time tomorrow, not at the same minute tomorrow — otherwise a * learner who studies a little earlier each morning gets "practice" on every * card the UI promised was due.

notes.title: Three on-time answers: ease 2.8, interval 8
notes.body:
Start: ease 2.5. Each correct answer adds 0.1 to ease (capped at 2.8). Answer 1: ease 2.6, interval 1 day. Answer 2: ease 2.7, interval 3 days. Answer 3: ease 2.8, and now the interval is `round(state.intervalDays * next.ease)` = round(3 x 2.8) = round(8.4) = **8**. The key detail the walkthrough stresses: the multiplier is the **already raised** ease, `next.ease`, not the old `state.ease`.

Why the others are wrong:
- **ease 2.8, interval 7**: round(3 x 2.5) would use the old ease; the code uses `next.ease`.
- **ease 2.7, interval 8**: ease moves on every correct answer, including the first, so three answers give 2.8.
- **ease 2.5, interval 9**: ease is not frozen until a lapse, and intervals multiply by ease, not triple.

excerpts.quote: next.ease = Math.min(MAX_EASE, state.ease + 0.1); if (next.reps === 1) next.intervalDays = 1; else if (next.reps === 2) next.intervalDays = 3; else next.intervalDays = Math.round(state.intervalDays * next.ease);
The multiplier is the *already raised* ease (`next.ease`, not `state.ease`).

notes.title: The key never left the server, but its position did
notes.body:
ADR-0002 made sure the answer's **value** never reached the browser. But the choices were sent in the order the author wrote them, and authors had put the right choice second in 363 of 389 multiple-choice and output questions. So "always press 2" scored 93% without ever seeing the key. The ADR says it plainly: the decision protected the key's value and ignored its position. ADR-0014 fixes it by shuffling the choices on every serve and grading by choice id, so position carries no information.

Why the others are wrong:
- **choice length, fixed by padding**: length is not the leak the ADR names.
- **response timing**: no timing leak is described.
- **the explanation sent early**: `why` is stripped along with `answer` before a question leaves the server.

excerpts.quote: Choices are sent in authored order, and the key is index 1 in 363 of 389 mcq/output questions. "Always press 2" scores 93% (server B1, register M-01). The decision protected the key's value and ignored its position. ADR-0014 fixes this by shuffling on every serve and grading by choice id.

notes.title: Why isDue needs attempts > 0
notes.body:
A card that has never been answered still needs a `dueAt` value, because the column is `NOT NULL`. `emptyCardState` sets it to `new Date(0)`, which is 1 January 1970, meaning "long ago". The date comparison alone would therefore say every unseen card is overdue. The `attempts > 0` part is what keeps unseen cards out of review. Drop it and review mode becomes the whole curriculum; the walkthrough says the dashboard would show 434 due. The guard and the default are one decision split across two files.

Why the others are wrong:
- **only wrongly answered cards**: those are due in 10 minutes anyway; the breakage is about unseen cards.
- **an unseen card stores null**: it stores the 1970 epoch, not null.
- **mastered cards stop coming due**: removing a guard cannot make fewer cards due.

excerpts.quote: `emptyCardState` sets `dueAt: new Date(0).toISOString()`, which is 1970-01-01. A column declared `NOT NULL` needs a value, and the epoch is "long ago". Without the `attempts > 0` guard, every unseen question would be due
return state.attempts > 0 && new Date(state.dueAt) <= now;

notes.title: Why the third interval has a floor of one day
notes.body:
The comment right above the line explains it. A card's state can arrive through import with `reps >= 2` but `intervalDays` 0. On the next correct answer, `0 * ease` is 0. Then `dueAt` would be the start of **today**, which is earlier than the answer that was just given. The card would be due again immediately, every time, and would never leave "due". `Math.max(1, ...)` makes the shortest interval one day.

Why the others are wrong:
- **scheduled the same day near midnight**: that is not the case the comment describes; the problem is a zero interval from import.
- **negative intervals from low ease**: ease is floored at 1.3, so it is never negative.
- **the 180-day cap bypassed**: the cap is the `Math.min` part, which stays in place either way.

excerpts.quote: // Floor at one day: a state that arrived through import can carry // `reps >= 2` with `intervalDays` 0, and `0 * ease` would put the card // due at today's midnight, before this answer, so it never leaves "due".

notes.title: The price of server-side grading
notes.body:
If only the server knows the key, the browser must send every answer to the server and wait for the result. ADR-0002 lists that as a cost: every answer is a round trip, so **there is no offline mode**. Its "Revisit when" section says what an offline mode would need: **signed, deferred grading**, where the result is computed and verified later, not shipping the key to the client.

Why the others are wrong:
- **CPU-bound grading**: the ADR says grading is a switch over six types and costs nothing.
- **choices cannot be shuffled**: shuffling happens on the server; it is the fix for the position leak.
- **answers can no longer be explained**: the explanation is returned with the graded result.

excerpts.quote: Cost: every answer is a round trip, so there is no offline mode.
An offline mode is required. Then the client needs signed, deferred grading, not the key.
Grading is a `switch` over six types and costs nothing.

notes.title: A lapse needs a card that was learned
notes.body:
A lapse means "you knew this and forgot it". Getting a brand-new question wrong the first time is not forgetting; you never knew it. So the code only adds to `lapses` when the card already had at least one correct rep: `state.lapses + (state.reps > 0 ? 1 : 0)`. The outcome names it too: a wrong answer with reps above 0 is `lapsed`, with reps of 0 it is `failed`.

Why the others are wrong:
- **both**: both reset reps, but only the learned card counts a lapse.
- **neither, only mastered cards**: one correct rep is enough; mastery (two reps) is not required.
- **only the first-ever wrong answer**: it is the other way round; the first-ever miss is the one that is not a lapse.

excerpts.quote: // Only count a lapse if the card had actually been learned — getting a new // question wrong the first time is not forgetting. const outcome = state.reps > 0 ? 'lapsed' : 'failed'; next.lapses = state.lapses + (state.reps > 0 ? 1 : 0);

notes.title: Why not just stop serving cards early
notes.body:
"Never serve a card before it is due" fixes the symptom in one place but fails twice. It **removes practice**: module drills and "Another round" deliberately show cards that are not due, and learners want that. And it **does not protect the API**: the scheduling rule lives where every answer passes, in `schedule()`; a client could still call the answer endpoint directly to farm reps. That is why the fix went into `schedule()` itself.

Why the others are wrong:
- **the relearn would be impossible**: relearn cards are due again 10 minutes after a miss, so they would still be served.
- **sessions run out of cards**: not the reason the ADR gives.
- **the client caches questions**: the ADR's point is the API, not a client cache.

excerpts.quote: **Never serve non-due cards.** It removes practice and still leaves the API able to farm reps.
Sessions deliberately re-serve non-due cards (module drills, "Another round"), so this was the normal path.

notes.title: Why farmed XP dropped without any migration
notes.body:
XP is **never stored**. It is recalculated by replaying each question's attempt log through `schedule()` and adding up `xpFor` for every outcome. When the practice rule shipped, the replay started classifying old early repeats as `practice`, which earns 1 XP instead of 6 or 10. So learners who had farmed repeats saw their XP drop once at upgrade, even though no column was changed. The ADR lists this as a known cost.

Why the others are wrong:
- **a 365-day replay window**: no such window is described; the change is in how each attempt is scored.
- **a migration deleted attempts**: no attempts were deleted; the log is replayed as-is.
- **a session cache invalidated**: there is no stored or cached XP to invalidate.

excerpts.quote: because XP is replayed from the log (ADR-0004 as amended by J14), learners who farmed repeats before this change see their XP drop once, at upgrade.
XP is never stored, so it cannot drift from the answers * that produced it, and replaying is what lets "practice earns 1" apply to * history without an `outcome` column.

notes.title: Why not FSRS
notes.body:
FSRS is a newer scheduling algorithm that predicts retention better than SM-2. ADR-0009 admits that, and still rejects it: FSRS works by fitting parameters to a learner's history of reviews, and **this app does not have those review logs yet**. The ADR does plan for later: it already stores `elapsedMs` and `answered_at`, so once months of attempts exist, the constants can be fitted rather than guessed.

Why the others are wrong:
- **cannot represent the 10-minute relearn**: not the stated reason.
- **non-commercial licence**: licensing is not mentioned.
- **needs a 0-5 self-rating**: that is the objection to full SM-2, a different rejected alternative.

excerpts.quote: **FSRS.** It is better at predicting retention, but it needs parameters fitted from review logs this app does not yet have.
With months of attempts, the constants (1, 3, ±0.1, 1.3–2.8) can be fitted instead of guessed. `elapsedMs` and `answered_at` are already stored for that.
